all.markdown:
# City Council Approves $480 Million Seawall Plan After Years of Flood Warnings

The 11-2 vote clears the way for construction to begin next spring along four miles of the eastern waterfront.

Sept. 14, 2026, 6:30 a.m. ET Updated Sept. 14, 2026, 3:12 p.m. ET

[312 comments](#comments)

The City Council voted 11-2 late Monday to approve a $480 million seawall along the eastern waterfront, ending a debate that has stalled through three mayoral administrations and at least five major floods.

The project will raise roughly four miles of shoreline between the Pierce Street ferry terminal and the mouth of Mill Creek by an average of six feet, using a combination of concrete flood walls, raised parkland and deployable gates at street ends. Construction is scheduled to begin next spring and to finish in 2031.

City engineers told the council that the neighborhoods behind the wall, home to about 38,000 residents, have flooded at high tide eleven times since 2019. A 2024 study commissioned by the city estimated that a single storm comparable to the one that struck in October 2023 would now cause more than $1.2 billion in damage.

About two-thirds of the cost will be covered by federal resilience grants awarded last year, according to the city's budget office. The remainder is expected to come from a bond measure that voters approved in 2025 and from a new stormwater fee on commercial properties that takes effect in January.

The two dissenting members, Councilors Robert Hale and Teresa Amundsen, argued that the design does too little for the low-lying blocks south of Mill Creek, which are outside the project boundary. Ms. Amundsen said her district would be "left holding the water that the wall pushes away" and asked for a study of how the barrier could shift flooding onto unprotected areas.

The city's chief resilience officer, Marcus Delgado, said modeling done for the project showed no measurable increase in flood depth south of the creek, but acknowledged that the second phase of the plan, which would extend protection to those blocks, has no funding yet.

Waterfront business owners largely supported the measure. Several told the council that repeated flooding had made it difficult to renew insurance policies, and that two restaurants on Harbor Row closed this summer after their premiums tripled.

Environmental groups were split. The Eastside Shoreline Alliance praised the inclusion of 22 acres of new tidal marsh in front of the wall, while the regional chapter of a national conservation group warned that hard barriers can accelerate erosion and urged the city to commit to monitoring the marsh for at least a decade.

The council also directed the city to hold quarterly public meetings during construction and to publish a dashboard tracking spending and progress. The first contracts are expected to be awarded in February, officials said.

_Priya Nair contributed reporting._
